subsections.subsection_title: What the OSCE station may say

blocks.text: “You are the doctor in the pediatric clinic. Take a focused history from the mother of a 3-year-old child presenting with cough and difficulty breathing.”
“Take a complete pediatric history from the mother of this child.”
Or you may be given a specific complaint:
The structure remains essentially the same, but you adapt your questions to the presenting complaint.
Smile, introduce yourself and establish who you are speaking to.
“Good morning. My name is Dr ____. I am one of the doctors looking after your child.”
“Could I please confirm your name and your relationship to the child?”

items: “Could I confirm your child's name and age, please?”

blocks.text: “I'd like to ask you some questions about your child and then, if appropriate, examine them. Is that okay?”
Do not immediately start firing questions at the parent.

subsections.subsection_title: Observe the child while taking the history

blocks.text: This is something candidates often forget.
While the caregiver is talking, look at the child.
Is the child small for age?
Does the child make eye contact?
If the child appears acutely unwell, you should not continue taking a leisurely history. Assess ABCDE and seek urgent assistance.
“This is a 4-year-old (yoruba, muslim) male child, John, brought by his mother, who is the primary caregiver and appears to be a reliable historian.”
A parent may not know certain details if they are not the primary caregiver.

items: “What brought your child to the hospital today?”

blocks.text: Allow the caregiver to speak without immediately interrupting.
Then establish the presenting complaints in the caregiver's own words.
“Fever for 3 days, cough for 2 days and difficulty breathing since this morning.”
Don't start converting the parent's description into a diagnosis.
“What symptoms have you noticed that made you think he has pneumonia?”
This is where you need to become complaint-specific.

items: “Can you tell me what happened from the beginning?”

blocks.text: But do not mechanically use SOCRATES for every pediatric complaint.
For example, in a child with fever, the more important questions are:

items: “Is it continuous or does it come and go?”
“What have you given the child for the fever?”

blocks.text: Sudden cough following choking = think foreign body aspiration.
“When did you first notice that the child was having difficulty breathing?”
“Can the baby breastfeed normally or does the baby have to stop to breathe?”
That is an excellent pediatric question.
This is an extremely common OSCE scenario.
Ask the caregiver to describe exactly what happened.
How long before returning to normal?

items: “Was the child completely back to normal after the episode?”

blocks.text: This helps distinguish different causes and characterize the event.

items: HIV or other chronic infections where relevant
“Has your child ever been admitted to hospital before?”
“Is your child currently taking any medications?”

blocks.text: “Does your child have any allergies to medications, food or anything else?”
You need to know whether it caused:
This is extremely important in pediatrics, particularly for infants, developmental problems and neurological presentations.
This is particularly important in infants and nutritional/developmental cases.
How frequently does the baby breastfeed?
What the child consumed within the last 24 hours before presenting to the hospital.

items: “Is your child's immunization up to date?”
“Do you have the child's immunization card?”

blocks.text: If the station requires detail, ask about specific vaccines according to the relevant national schedule.
You don't necessarily need to perform a complete developmental assessment during every history, but you should establish whether development has been appropriate.
“Have you noticed any delay compared with other children of the same age?”
“Has your child ever acquired a skill and subsequently lost it?”
This identifies developmental regression, which is a major red flag.

items: “Has the child been gaining weight appropriately?”
“Are the parents related to each other by blood?”

blocks.text: This can be particularly relevant when investigating congenital or inherited disorders.
For adolescents, you may need to take a more confidential history.
Explain confidentiality appropriately, including its limits where there is a serious safety concern.
“Thank you. Is there anything else about your child's illness that you think is important and that I haven't asked about?”
“Do you have any particular concerns or questions about your child?”

subsections.subsection_title: How to present the history to the examiner

blocks.text: Don't simply repeat everything you asked.

items: (vi). OCCUPATION: Mother is a petty trader

blocks.text: I present Mary John, a 3 year old infant, who is a Christian Langei and lives at Gindiri, Jos, Plateau state. She presented 2 days ago at the Emergency Pediatric Unit; with a 1week 2 day history of fever, a 4 day history of yellow discoloration of the eye and a 2 day history of vomiting.

The fever started 1 week and 2 days prior to presentation, it started in the afternoon after school and it was high grade and intermittent, with each paroxysm of fever lasting about 6 to 8 hours and a period of respite of about 18 to 24 hours. It was temporarily relieved by taking paracetamol and tepid sponging. There is no known aggravating factor. It was not associated with excessive crying , nor was it associated with convulsion nor fainting. There was also no eye, nose nor ear discharge. It was not associated with chills nor was it associated with rigors. It was associated yellowing of the eyes and vomiting , no abdominal pain. It was not associated any weight loss, no difficulty in micturition, nor pain during micturition, around the flanks nor around the private part. There was no discharge anywhere in the body.

The yellow discoloration of the eye was noticed about 6 days ago when her mother was giving her a bath, she said it appeared light yellow and that it did not extend past the eyes but that it increased in shade since it was noticed. It is associated with loss of appetite, no abdominal pain nor abdominal distension. She is not a known sickle cell disease patient.No diarrhea but she started vomiting about 4 days ago
[VOMITING – onset/timing e.g. post-tussive, nausea, projectile, frequency, relation to position and/or feeding].

She started vomiting about 4 days ago, the vomiting is associated with nausea and usually follows meals, it was non projectile, She has about 2 bouts of vomiting per day and it is not related to her posture. The last episode of vomiting was this morning [about 2 hours ago]. The nausea is reduced when she drinks fanta lemon. [It was not associated with wretching – the age].
[VOMITUS – quantity, content, color, blood stained or bilous, smell].
The vomitus was about 6mls and contained recently ingested food. It was yellowish in color, not bloody, non bilous and it was not foamy nor foul smelling.

There was associated yellow discoloration of the eye and loss of appetite but it was not associated with weight loss, loose stools, no abdominal pain, no abdominal distension, no excessive bowel sounds nor did she have a gaseous stomach.
WHAT HAS BEEN DONE FOR HER.

Since admission 2 days ago, blood, urine, vomitus and stool samples have been taken for investigations but her mother does not know the results of these tests and she was put on intravenous fluids and some drugs [Artesunate and Lumefantrine syrup, vitamin B, Paracetamol syrup], she has also been given 3 injections since admission. Her health has since admission improved as evidenced by her increased appetite and reduced fever.
No headache, blurring vision, nor convulsion. She is not a known epileptic

items: No cough,difficulty in breathing nor chest pain

blocks.text: No easy fatiguability, nor does she feel an unusual sensation of her heart beating
No flank pains, nor difficulty and pain during micturition, there was no discharge of any sort from any part of the body, no itching, no increased frequency, no itching around the private part.
She has never been admitted in the hospital, nor has she been transfused with blood. She is not a known diabetic, hypertensive nor is she a known sickle cell disease patient.

She reacts to chloroquin by itching, she does not use any form of herbal medication and is currently on medication for her current illness. She is not on any form of chronic medication [for chronic asthma, epilepsy, Hypertension, I.D.D.M].

Her mother booked her pregnancy when she was about 4 months gestation here at the Jos University Teaching Hospital, she was faithful to her antenatal clinic visits, she took all her drugs and has had all her TT vaccines. She never fell sick during the pregnancy and did not have any problems with the pregnancy.

She delivered at term here at JUTH, without any complications. the baby cried immediately but she does not remember the APGAR score of the baby. The cord was cut with a sterile pair of scissors, and was cleaned with methylated spirit and cotton wool. The baby did not have any problems and started breast feeding immediately. Both mother and child were discharged the following day after birth and both had no problems during the puerperal period.

Baby started breast feeding about 30 minutes after birth, the baby fed well and was breast fed on demand. She cannot confirm the quantity of breast milk the baby consumed. Her mother sometimes used to express the breast milk, and whenever she expressed the breast milk, the baby was fed with cup and spoon. All remainder was properly heated and recooled before it was given to the baby.

The baby was exclusively breastfed and weaning commenced at the age 6 months and 9 days. Maize, ground nut and soya bean gruel was used to wean the baby, mother usually washed her hands before preparing the baby’s meals, she fortified the gruel with powdered milk. The baby adjusted well, and started eating family diet when she was 1 year old. She eats at least 3 times daily and does not eat outside the house.
She ate bread and egg, with an orange and a cup of tea yesterday morning, fried rice and fish in the afternoon and semovita with vegetable soup and meat last night.
She was given; HBV1, OPV0, BCG at birth and she has a BCG scar on her left upper arm.
At 6 weeks she was given; HBV2, OPV1 and DPT1.
At 10 weeks she was given; OPV2 and DPT2.
At 14 weeks she was given; HBV3, OPV3 and DPT3.
At 9 months she was given; Vitamin A1 and Measles vaccine.

items: At 15 months she was given; Vitamin A2
She had palmar grasp of objects
10 months – Could Stand and walk with support
She had a Vocabulary of about 5 words

blocks.text: 24 months [2 years] – Could Put on shoes by her self
30 months [2 and a half years] – She could Recognize colors

She is the 2nd of 3 siblings born to a monogamous home, the 1st is a boy of 6 years and the 3rd is a 1 year old girl. Her father is a 30 year old Secondary school teacher and her mother is a 28 year old tailor. Non of her siblings nor her parents have suffered similar illness, there is no family history of asthma, epilepsy, hypertension, diabetes nor sickle cell disease.

Father and mother do not smoke cigarette nor do they drink alcohol, they live in a two bedroom flat, and she sleeps with her other siblings in a room, the room has 2 windows which measures about 4 by 4 feet, the windows and doors are not netted and she does not sleep with a mosquito net, her mother said she does not like it. The house is seldom fumigated with insecticide, the kitchen is not attached to the house and they use firewood as cooking fuel, she does not stay with her mother in the kitchen, they make use of a pit latrine and get their drinking water from a neighborhood well. They practice open dumping of refuse and sullage. They do not rear any domestic animals within their vicinity.

I present Miss Joana Cup, a 3 year old infant who presented 2 days ago at the Emergency Pediatric Unit; with a 1week 2 day history of fever, a 4 day history of yellow discoloration of the eye and a 2 day history of vomiting. She is currently being managed here at J.U.T.H. and has recorded considerable improvement in her health as evidenced by a reduction in her fever and a marked increase in appetite.

items: EXAMPLE 2: WHEN EXAMINER ASKS YOU TO SUMMARIZE

blocks.text: “This is a 4-year-old boy who was brought by his mother, who is a reliable historian, with a 3-day history of fever associated with cough and a 1-day history of difficulty breathing. The fever was measured at home and was associated with reduced appetite. There was no history of convulsion, vomiting, diarrhoea or rash. The cough was non-productive, with no history of choking or previous similar episodes.

He has no known chronic medical illness and is not on regular medications. There is no known drug allergy. He was born at term via spontaneous vaginal delivery with no significant perinatal complications. His immunizations are reportedly up to date and his development has been appropriate for age.
There is no significant family history of asthma, sickle cell disease or congenital heart disease. There are no known TB contacts.

My initial impression is an acute febrile respiratory illness, with pneumonia among the differentials. I would proceed to examine the child, particularly assessing the general condition, hydration, respiratory system and cardiovascular system.”
That is the level of concise, clinically meaningful presentation you want.

subsections.subsection_title: The Pediatric History Framework to Memorize

blocks.text: INTRO → PC → HPC → PMH → DRUGS/ALLERGIES → BIRTH → FEEDING → IMMUNIZATION → DEVELOPMENT → GROWTH → ELIMINATION → FAMILY → SOCIAL → SCHOOL/ADOLESCENT → ROS → CONCERNS → SUMMARY
You don't have to ask every question in every station.
The key is to adapt the history to the presenting complaint.

content_groups.group_title: Q: Who should provide the history?

blocks.text: Answer: The parent or primary caregiver usually provides the history, but the child should be involved directly when their age and developmental level allow.

content_groups.group_title: Q: What makes pediatric history different from adult history?

blocks.text: “The history is often obtained from a parent or caregiver, developmental and birth histories are particularly important, and the child's growth, nutrition, immunization and family/social environment must be assessed.”

content_groups.group_title: Q: What is the most important part of pediatric history?

blocks.text: There isn't one single component. It depends on the presentation.
For an acutely ill child, severity and red flags come first.
For developmental concerns, developmental, birth and neurological history become particularly important.

content_groups.group_title: Q: What would make you stop taking the history?

blocks.text: If the child appears critically ill, for example:
You should prioritize ABCDE assessment and emergency management.

content_groups.group_title: Q: Why is birth history important?

blocks.text: Because antenatal, perinatal and neonatal events can provide important clues to:

content_groups.group_title: Q: Why ask about developmental regression?

blocks.text: Because loss of previously acquired skills is abnormal and may indicate neurological, metabolic, genetic or neurodegenerative disease.
To establish protection against vaccine-preventable diseases and identify missed vaccines or opportunities for catch-up vaccination.
Before leaving the station, mentally ask:

C — Complaint H — History of complaint P — Past medical & surgical history D — Drugs/allergies B — Birth history F — Feeding I — Immunization D — Development G — Growth E — Elimination F — Family history S — Social/environment S — School/adolescent R — Review of systems C — Concerns

content_groups.group_title: The examiner should come away knowing

blocks.text: Who is the child? What is wrong? How sick are they? What caused it? What relevant background factors exist? And what needs to happen next?
That is the essence of a good pediatric history.
